extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students or general readers studying American government, politics, and the judicial system
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter-level survey of the judicial system and of substantive private and public law topics (property, torts, contracts, domestic relations, procedure, and crimes). Explains definitions, classifications, procedural steps, remedies, and policy considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codification vs common law — considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of attempts by states to codify the civil law and the major objections to codification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages cited (uniform statutes like negotiable instruments law adopted by many states) and disadvantages listed: a code cannot foresee every contingency so must be general and elastic (leading to litigation over interpretation); codification crystallizes and increases diversity among state laws by legislative amendment; codification removes judicial flexibility to adapt law to new conditions, leaving modifications to legislatures which may lead to constant tinkering and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of civil law vs criminal law
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil law's purpose is to protect the rights of the individual and to redress his wrongs; criminal law's purpose is to punish and prevent public wrongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the difference in aims and consequences (private redress vs public punishment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of individual rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual rights are classified under three heads: the right of personal security, the right of personal liberty, and the right of private property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that private property is the most complicated and receives extended treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real property and estates — definitions and types
rubrics_metrics.description: Real property consists of land and rights connected with land; estates (interests) in land are of various kinds: estate in fee simple (highest, nearly absolute ownership), life estate, estates for years, conditional estates, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains freehold (fee simple, life estate) vs estates less than freehold (estate for years); examples include curtesy and dower; estates may commence in the future or be conditional (e.g., life estate conditioned on remaining unmarried).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal property — four classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal property is divided into: (1) chattels real (leases of lands or buildings), (2) tangible personalty (watches, clothing, etc.), (3) choses in action (claims against debtors, notes, stocks, bonds), and (4) intellectual/property rights (trade-marks, copyrights).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorizes typical items and legal rights that form personal property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Torts — definition and threefold classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Torts are violations of private rights; they may be subdivided into (a) torts directed against the person, (b) torts aimed at property, and (c) torts affecting both person and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides organizational framework for considering particular torts and remedies (suit for damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: False imprisonment
rubrics_metrics.description: False imprisonment consists in arresting or detaining a person without sufficient cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classified as a tort directed against the person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malicious prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who maliciously and without probable cause institutes proceedings against another is guilty of malicious prosecution, provided the original action has terminated in favor of the injured party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires malice, lack of probable cause, and favorable termination for the victim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assault and battery distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting another in fear of personal injury is an assault; inflicting violence upon him constitutes a battery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the two related but distinct torts against the person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation — libel vs slander
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation of character occurs in two forms: libel (expressed in print or writing) and slander (oral defamation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out the media distinction for defamation actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trespass and deceit (property torts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trespass upon land is unauthorized entry on another's land; trespass to goods is wrongfully taking or destroying personal property; deceit is knowingly making a false statement on which another relies and is damaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies the conduct that constitutes these property torts and the element of reliance/damage for deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuisance
rubrics_metrics.description: Any disturbance of another's reasonable use and enjoyment of his own property constitutes a nuisance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include smelting works giving off odors, unreasonable ringing of church bells, noises disturbing sleep; nuisance can affect person and property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negligence — duty of care
rubrics_metrics.description: Negligence consists in the failure to perform the duty of care which one owes to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reckless running of a railroad train resulting in an accident, negligent driving in a city, collapse of a building due to defective construction; negligence is actionable as a tort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses in tort — contributory negligence and fellow-servant rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributory negligence (plaintiff's negligence contributing to injury) is considered a complete defense; the fellow-servant rule may prevent recovery when an employee is injured by another employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that the fellow-servant rule has been abolished in some states for certain employments; explains the effect of these defenses on liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract formation — offer, acceptance, consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: To constitute a contract there must be an offer by one party and acceptance by the other; a valid contract must be made for a 'consideration' (each party gives up something).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: offer to sell a house and acceptance constitutes meeting of minds; a mere promise without exchange is not binding; contracts may be implied from transaction (e.g., ordering goods from a store implies promise to pay reasonable value).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts requiring written evidence (Statute of Frauds categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain contracts must be proved by written evidence before a court will enforce them: contracts for the sale of real estate, sale of goods over a certain amount, contracts not to be performed within a year, and a few others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the limited exceptions to the general rule that oral agreements can be binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiable instruments — holder in due course rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Negotiable instruments (promissory notes, drafts, checks) have the characteristic that if one obtained the instrument by fraud and cannot sue on it, a transferee who takes it for value and without knowledge of the fraud may enforce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated purpose: to facilitate dealings among merchants and bankers; explains the special protection for transferees for value who are ignorant of prior fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bailments — definition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Bailments consist in the delivery of personal property to another for some particular and temporary purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lending a book to a friend, giving a watch for repair, pawning jewelry, depositing goods in a storage warehouse, shipping goods by freight/express.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurance contracts — common forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies of insurance (life, fire, marine, accident, etc.) form a large class of contracts with their own rules and importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies insurance as a distinct and commonly litigated category of contractual relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies — damages at law and specific performance in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual remedy at law for breach of contract is money damages; equity may order specific performance (ordering a party to carry out a contract), but such relief is limited to certain classes of contracts (principally agreements for sale of real estate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity relief takes many forms (decrees commanding action or injunctions); failure to obey equity decrees is contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic relations — marriage formalities and annulment grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern law generally requires formal solemnization of marriages; marriages between close relatives or by persons below a certain age are void; marriages induced by fraud or duress may be declared void at the instance of the injured party; mental or physical incapacity is a ground for annulment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes historic common-law rules and modern statutory modifications; outlines basic void/voidable grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Married women's property rights — historical rule and modification
rubrics_metrics.description: At common law, personal property of a woman became the property of the husband on marriage, and married women were often incapable of making binding contracts; these rules have been modified throughout the U.S., and in advanced commonwealths married women now have substantially the same property rights as men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains evolution from common-law disabilities toward modern parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divorce grounds and interstate recognition problems
rubrics_metrics.description: All states except one (South Carolina at time of text) allow absolute divorce; grounds vary greatly among states (from adultery only to incompatibility or abandonment), and easy divorce in some states may not be recognized elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentions movement to secure uniformity in divorce laws and the political controversy surrounding liberal vs conservative divorce regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance — intestacy, wills, executors and administrators
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules govern distribution of real and personal property when a person dies intestate; where a will exists, the law provides for enforcement and disposition; executors (named) or administrators (appointed) take charge of estate distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes variation among states and separate rules for real vs personal property in many jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporations and associations — principal distinctions from partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Associations take principal forms as partnerships and corporations; partnership existence depends on partners' lives, may require unanimity for important actions, partners are generally liable for all partnership debts and interests are not freely transferable; corporations are permanent, governed by majority rule for decisions, shareholders usually have liability limited to par value and shares are freely transferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes key organizational and liability differences shaping legal treatment of business associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil procedure — commencing a suit and pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: A suit is usually commenced by a plaintiff's complaint or declaration served with a summons; defendant may demur (challenge sufficiency of facts) or answer/plea (deny facts or set up affirmative defenses); an interchange of pleadings continues until an issue is reached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes differences in states with common-law procedure (multiple pleadings) vs code systems that frequently limit steps to complaint and answer (sometimes reply allowed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial procedure — judge and jury roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity suits are tried by a judge alone; suits at law are generally tried before a judge and jury (unless jury waived). The judge regulates trial conduct and rules on matters of law; the jury decides questions of fact under the judge's guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains sequence: opening statements, direct/cross-examination, rebuttal/surrebuttal, closing addresses, judge's charge, jury deliberation and verdict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury selection and challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurors are summoned and examined by opposing counsel; jurors legally exempt or incompetent (bias, etc.) may be excused by the judge; each side may challenge a certain number of jurors without stating cause (peremptory challenges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out basic voir dire and challenge mechanisms used to form an impartial jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of evidence and reversal on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions at trial are strictly regulated by complicated rules of evidence; an error by the judge in admitting improper evidence or excluding competent testimony is ground for reversal of judgment on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the centrality of admissibility and proper evidentiary rulings to appellate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed verdicts, dismissals, and verdict requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff fails to make out a prima facie case the judge may dismiss the complaint without sending it to the jury; if only one conclusion of fact is possible, the judge may direct the jury to return a verdict accordingly; verdicts in most states must be unanimous and a hung jury leads to retrial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains judicial control over submission to jury and consequences (dismissal, directed verdict, retrial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of masters or referees in complicated cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In complicated cases it is customary to send them to a master or referee to take testimony and make a tentative finding; the judge reviews the record and the report and makes a final decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes procedural device to manage complex fact-finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution and enforcement of judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment for damages is entered; if defendant does not pay, an execution may be issued authorizing the sheriff to take possession and sell enough property at auction to satisfy the judgment and costs; for disputes over real estate title, the usual judgment may be that the plaintiff enter upon the premises and the sheriff may evict resisting defendants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains practical steps for enforcement and the limits (no redress if defendant has no property).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity decrees and contempt for noncompliance
rubrics_metrics.description: A decree in equity orders the defendant to do or not do something (specific performance, injunctions); failure to obey a decree is contempt of court and may lead to fines or imprisonment until compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights the coercive nature of equitable remedies and contempt sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals — grounds, process, and policy concerns about delay
rubrics_metrics.description: A losing party may appeal for errors of law or because the verdict was contrary to the weight of evidence; appellate courts usually pass only on questions of law; appeals may be repeated up to highest courts and can produce long delays (example of a case with many retrials spanning 20 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses policy trade-offs: restricting appeals could deny justice; allowing appeals only by permission risks injustice; appellate courts have power to enter final judgment though rarely exercised; encouraging final disposition by appellate courts when possible could reduce delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal law classification — felonies and misdemeanors
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes are divided into felonies (graver offences generally punished by death or confinement in state's prison) and misdemeanors (lesser offences punished by fines or short imprisonment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes collateral consequences (e.g., loss of right to vote on felony conviction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of principal felonies (murder, manslaughter, arson, burglary, robbery, larceny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Murder: intentional killing; manslaughter: unintentional killing (including heat of passion with adequate provocation). Arson: wilful and malicious burning of a dwelling-house (any incendiarism suffices). Burglary: breaking and entering another's house with intent to commit a felony (breaking/entering itself suffices). Robbery: taking property from a person or in his presence by force. Larceny: stealing personal property (grand vs petty depending on amount).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains distinctions and examples illustrating each offense and degree distinctions in some states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other felonies — forgery, counterfeiting, kidnapping, bigamy, perjury
rubrics_metrics.description: Forgery: making or altering a written instrument to defraud another (e.g., signing another's name on a check). Counterfeiting (making false money) is federally punished. Kidnapping, bigamy (having more than one spouse at same time) and perjury (wilful false testimony under oath) are commonly felonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists additional crimes often classified as felonies and describes elements or examples.
